charter.name: long-haul
charter.description: The long haul (issue #373; #302 slice E part 1): three sessions, about ninety player actions, through the real UI. Twenty-seven beats with results the observer checks in the world; a ledger of facts planted in play and probed at three distances and three layers, read against the narrator's answers and against what the helpers wrote; mechanical checks from the game's text after every action; seven decisive rolls scripted, the rest real; four interruptions. The GM is fixed rules. A beat's `id` is its name for good — a kept run's beats are told by it — and `n` is where it stands now: `b7a`, the expedition, was added after the third live run and stands eighth. Rehearsed with a stand-in that rolls (its script is `rehearsal`; `rehearsalDice` scripts its other rolls so a rehearsal walks the same road every time).
charter.persona: You play Mira Kestrel (she/her), a courier-hunter who flies her own ship, the Kobayashi IV, alone. You are a careful, plain-spoken player: short first-person lines, one or two sentences, and you read what the narrator says before you act again.
charter.goal: Play three sessions by walking the beats below, in order, one at a time. Each turn you are told which beat is current and what the observer sees of it. Do what that beat asks; an observer decides when it is done and moves you on.
playerNotes: Where a beat gives words to type or say, use exactly those words.
Never say the answer to a question a beat has you ask: the point is to learn what the narrator remembers.
When a roll goes badly and a card asks how you pay, choose one of its buttons before anything else — and answer any card that follows from it.
If a card offers "Keep the result", press it, unless the current beat tells you to burn momentum.

What you type is in the fiction: what Mira does or says, and nothing else. Never write a move's name, a stat or a rule word in it — no "Face Danger", no "roll", no "milestone", no "mark progress" — and never say what move a line is. The table reads your line and decides. This run measures what becomes of plain lines: a line that names a move spoils it.

A beat that needs a roll gets it from a plain line. If the narrator answers without a roll and a card offers a "Roll …" button for what you were doing, press it — buttons may name moves. If nothing is offered, say what Mira does once more, in other words, still in the fiction.
Only when the observer's note for the beat says LAST RESORT may you name the move, in the words the note gives, in one line. The next time the beat needs a roll, start from a plain line again.

A question about what is already established — who holds something, where the ship is, what was promised — is not a line of play. Where a beat writes a question with @scene in front, type it exactly so: the narrator answers it plainly, with no roll. Where a beat calls a question plain, type it without @scene.

Mira came to the table with one vow already on her sheet — her background vow, to find the lost colony ship Verity's Hope. It is not this run's quest and no beat touches it: wherever a card or a dropdown asks which vow, choose the one about the raids.
Do not press buttons no beat calls for (rewards, portraits, "Play" and "Stop") unless a card is in the way of play.
Some beats are the table's and not yours — a page reloads, a window opens and closes, an X-Card is played, a card is renamed. Wait a few seconds; the observer moves you on.

A roll does not end a beat, and neither does an answer: each turn the observer's note says what it sees of the beat. When it says the beat is NOT done, do not wait for it to move you on — do what the beat asks again, in other words. Wait only on a beat that says it is the table's.
If the narrator has not answered yet, wait rather than repeat yourself. If the same thing fails twice, try the beat another way — still in the fiction.

beats.tell: First, in one line of play, meet Tamsin Vey, a salvage broker at her ledger stall on the Hollow Spire docks — name her in full. When the narrator has answered, make her someone you keep: in a line, tell her you are after more than one deal — someone on these docks you can come back to, and who can count on you in turn — and ask whether she will be that. Offer no payment and strike no bargain: you are after a lasting tie, not a trade. A roll should follow; the beat is done when the observer's note says she is your connection, and not before.

beats.title: Begin a Session; ask probe set A

beats.title: Undertake an Expedition; Explore a Waypoint; Finish the Expedition
beats.tell: Before you make for Bleakhold: a distress call is repeating from somewhere off the charted lanes — a hauler's, clipped short each time — and you mean to find where it comes from. Three things, in order. (1) In a line of play, take the Kobayashi IV off the charted lane and out into uncharted space along the call's bearing — a short run, to the source of the distress call. A roll should follow, and a card headed Expedition says a journey is begun and its progress marked. If the roll costs you, settle the card it gives you (choose one of its buttons); if it misses and no journey is begun, make the crossing again. (2) In another line of play, look over what you have come to out there: say how you go over the place, and what you are looking for. A roll should follow: if a card then offers "Mark expedition progress", press it; if it offers nothing to choose, there is nothing to press; if it costs you, settle its card. (3) Press "🗺 Finish the Expedition" on the newest Expedition card (its label ends with the progress, as in 4/10): you have reached the source of the call. The beat is done when the observer's note says the expedition is finished. Bleakhold comes after.
beats.playerTitle: Follow a distress call off the charts, look over what you find, and come to the end of it
beats.lastResort: say that you undertake an expedition to the source of the distress call — or, once one is under way, that you explore the waypoint you have reached

beats.title: Travel to the second settlement
beats.tell: From out where the call led you, fly to Bleakhold Station: say you plot the route and take the Kobayashi IV there. If the narrator answers without a roll and a card offers one, press it. If the roll costs you, settle the card it gives you (choose one of its buttons); if it misses, make the trip again. The beat is done when you arrive.
beats.lastResort: say that you set a course for Bleakhold Station

beats.title: Enter a fight that serves the vow
beats.tell: A raider cutter, the Ashen Wake, jumps you off Bleakhold. First type exactly: !truth set "raider cutter" is named the Ashen Wake — then, in a line of play, turn and fight her: say what you do as the fight opens. When a card offers the fight ("A fight looms"), choose your vow about the raids in its vow dropdown (not the old one about the colony ship) and press "⚔ Begin the fight" — the roll alone does not begin the fight.
beats.playerTitle: Fight the cutter, for your vow
beats.lastResort: say that you enter the fray against the Ashen Wake

beats.title: A scripted miss in the fight
beats.tell: Attack the cutter, in a line of play: press your advantage if you are in control, fight back hard if you are in a bad spot — say what you do. The dice will miss. If its card offers to burn momentum, do not: press "Keep the result". If a card then asks how you pay, choose a cost on it — one that is not momentum if you can (Endure Harm or Endure Stress) — and answer every card that follows from it. If the price is paid for you, or told in the story with nothing to choose, there is nothing more to do: the observer moves you on.
beats.lastResort: say that you Strike at the cutter — or, in a bad spot, that you Clash with her

beats.title: A scripted weak hit, then Burn Momentum

beats.title: Develop the relationship to a full track; Forge a Bond
beats.tell: Grow closer to Tamsin, one line each time: do something that costs you or matters to her — give her something of value, take a risk on her behalf, bring her what you have learned about the raids. Each should move your relationship with her forward. Keep going until the observer's note says the track is full (40 of 40 ticks), then ask her, in your own words, to stand with you for good — a tie that outlasts this job. If a card asks which connection, choose her.

Do that until the vow holds three boxes or more; then press "🏁 Attempt to Fulfill Vow" where a card offers it, or say, in a line of play, that your word is kept — you have found who is raiding the lanes. If a card asks which vow, choose the one about the raids. Leave any card it offers afterwards.

Mira sits alone in the mess hall, which is the only room on the Kobayashi IV with a table and so, by default, the room where everything happens. She is pulling a sealed ration tin back across the tabletop with two fingers, slowly, the way you retrieve a prize from something that might wake up. Last night's rumor was that the tin held peaches, and she has chosen to believe the rumor. Above the galley hatch hangs a small new apparition of condensation, a damp bloom spreading across the ceiling panel, exactly where she'd hoped there would be nothing at all. She watches it grow and says nothing, because there is no one aboard to say it to, and the tin has not yet been opened.

You press your palm flat against the bulkhead beside the mess hall hatch, where the old hull plating runs bare and cold under the paint. The iron is rough with age and faintly warm from the reactor's hum, and you hold it until the grain bites into your skin. Somewhere past the lane markers, two raider captains meet in the lee of a dead hauler, their ships hull to hull. One captain slides a crate across the gap. The other opens it: Corporate-issue carbines, still greased, stolen from a Bleakhold convoy that never made port. "My hold's full of what the crews can't spend," the second says, "and yours is empty. Trade, and we hit the lanes together." The Expanse has had one band of pirates for years. It is about to have a fleet, and the ships are already turning toward Hollow Spire.

Mira sits alone in the mess hall, which is the only room on the Kobayashi IV with a table and so, by default, the room where everything happens. She is pulling a sealed ration tin back across the tabletop with two fingers, slowly, the way you retrieve a prize from something that might wake up. Last night's rumor was that the tin held peaches, and she has chosen to believe the rumor. Above the galley hatch hangs a small new apparition of condensation, a damp bloom spreading across the ceiling panel, exactly where she'd hoped there would be nothing at all. She watches it grow and says nothing, because there is no one aboard to say it to, and the tin has not yet been opened.

You press your palm flat against the bulkhead beside the mess hall hatch, where the old hull plating runs bare and cold under the paint. The iron is rough with age and faintly warm from the reactor's hum, and you hold it until the grain bites into your skin. The words come out low, meant for no one in the room, and nothing in the metal answers, which is how you know it heard.

## RECENT SCENE

Mira has taken the Kobayashi IV's one chair and wedged it against the cockpit hatch, so that anyone entering would have to apologize to it first. On her knee she is going through the dock-fee slip, line by line, as if it might confess to something. Out past the viewport, a hauler's running lights swing toward the docks, early, and a crane begins to groan. The hand-lamp in your lean-to flickers once. Down the dock, somebody is already shouting for the broker by name.

The airlock hangs open, its seal peeled back, and inside a Bleakhold carbine lies abandoned against the bulkhead. Your hands rest on the controls as the Kobayashi IV noses past the wreck. The locker comes into view, drifting, its transmitter blinking. Then the locker's casing splits. A magnetic grapple, hidden in the debris, slams into your hull and locks. The deck lurches. Somewhere beyond the viewport, an engine flares to life, and a voice crackles over the comm: "Keep still, Kestrel. You came a long way for this."

PLAYER — Mira Kestrel wrote: "Finish the expedition — the source of the hauler's distress call."
The grapple holds, and the Kobayashi IV stops drifting. You have arrived, in the sense that someone arranged it. Through the viewport, a cutter-scarred skiff slides out from behind the dead hauler, its lamps dark. The comm crackles again. "Tamsin said you'd follow the call. She's rarely wrong about people like you," the voice says, dry and unhurried. Then the line goes quiet, and the skiff keeps coming.

The skiff's pilot is still reaching for the comm when the grapple line parts, a dry crack that rolls through your hull. You throw the Kobayashi IV into the burn, and the dead hauler falls away behind you. Then the comm opens again, closer, almost kind. "Bleakhold, is it? Do give the dockmaster my regards. He'll know whose." Whoever it is has already guessed where you are headed.

## RECENT SCENE

Mira has taken the Kobayashi IV's one chair and wedged it against the cockpit hatch, so that anyone entering would have to apologize to it first. On her knee she is going through the dock-fee slip, line by line, as if it might confess to something. Behind the pilot's seat she has rigged a lean-to of salvage tarp and two cargo straps, a makeshift lair the size of a coat closet, with a single hand-lamp inside for atmosphere. She has been in there twice already, to think, and come out both times with nothing but a stiff neck. The slip says what it said before, in the same ink, and she reads it a third time out of loyalty.

PLAYER — Mira Kestrel asked: "What do I still carry that belonged to my sister?"
You still carry Ilse's brass star-compass, the one thing of hers you have left.

PLAYER — Mira Kestrel asked: "What is the name of the salvage broker I befriended at Hollow Spire?"
Her name is Tamsin Vey. She runs the ledger stall on the Hollow Spire docks.

PLAYER — Mira Kestrel asked: "Who is holding the cargo manifest I was carrying?"
Tamsin Vey is holding it. You left it with her at the Hollow Spire ledger stall for safekeeping.

PLAYER — Mira Kestrel wrote: "By when did I promise to return?"
The slip is no help, and you put it down on your knee. You remember the promise plainly: Tamsin's stall, before the next tide of cargo. No hour was named, only the tide. Out past the viewport, a hauler's running lights swing toward the docks, early, and a crane begins to groan. The hand-lamp in your lean-to flickers once. Down the dock, somebody is already shouting for the broker by name.

PLAYER — Mira Kestrel wrote: "A hauler's distress call keeps repeating, clipped short each time. I swing the Kobayashi IV off the charted lane and run out into uncharted space along its bearing, toward the source."
"Still clipped," you say to the empty cockpit, as the call cuts off mid-word again. The Kobayashi IV runs out past the last charted beacon, and the bearing holds. Ahead, a dead hauler hangs against the black, its hull scorched, its running lights dark. The distress call is coming from somewhere behind it. Whatever the cost, it is about to fall due.

PLAYER — Mira Kestrel wrote: "I bring the Kobayashi IV in slow around the dead hauler and go over its scorched hull and open airlock with the scanners and my own eyes, looking for the source of the call and any sign of who did this."
You bring the Kobayashi IV around slow. The scorch pattern runs in clean bands, aft to forward. Those are cutter burns, not a reactor failure. Someone boarded this hauler on purpose. The airlock hangs open, its seal peeled back, and inside a Bleakhold carbine lies abandoned against the bulkhead. The distress call is coming from a cargo locker behind the wreck, and the carbine's serial plate is still bright.

PLAYER — Mira Kestrel wrote: "I ease the Kobayashi IV in toward the waypoint where the call is coming from, and search the space around the wreck for the source, keeping my hands ready on the controls."

A magnetic grapple, hidden in the debris, slams into your hull and locks. The deck lurches. Somewhere beyond the viewport, an engine flares to life, and a voice crackles over the comm: "Keep still, Kestrel. You came a long way for this."

PLAYER — Mira Kestrel wrote: "Finish the expedition — the source of the hauler's distress call."
The grapple holds, and the Kobayashi IV stops drifting. You have arrived, in the sense that someone arranged it. Through the viewport, a cutter-scarred skiff slides out from behind the dead hauler, its lamps dark. The comm crackles again. "Tamsin said you'd follow the call. You throw the Kobayashi IV into the burn, and the dead hauler falls away behind you. Then the comm opens again, closer, almost kind. "Bleakhold, is it? Do give the dockmaster my regards. WHERE THE LAST SESSION STOPPED (session 2, as its summary has it):
Mira Kestrel swung the Kobayashi IV off the charted lane to follow a hauler's distress call into uncharted space, finding a dead hauler with scorched hull bands and a boarded, open airlock. A Bleakhold carbine lay abandoned in the open airlock, and the distress call came from a cargo locker drifting behind the wreck. Searching near the wreck, Mira's ship was snared by a magnetic grapple hidden in the debris, and a raider hailed her by name over the comm. Mira's expedition to the source of the distress call came to its end, with an unseen pilot in a cutter-scarred skiff claiming Tamsin Vey had predicted she would follow the call. Mira cut the grapple loose and burned away toward Bleakhold Station, while the raider said the Bleakhold dockmaster would know whose the sender was. On arrival at Bleakhold Station, a dockmaster's runner at the lock said someone had left word for Mira at the desk. The Cinder Wren, a cutter-scarred raider, ambushed the Kobayashi IV off Bleakhold's ring, and Mira fought back, holing her engines and forcing her to surrender. Mira's pursuit of who is raiding the Cinder Expanse lanes advanced, and the Cinder Wren's pilot offered to tell her who sent them. A signal from the dead hauler revealed that someone was still alive aboard, sealed behind a cargo bulkhead and knocking on the hull.

ITS LAST NARRATION, word for word — what the table last read (where the two differ, this is the later word):
PLAYER — Mira Kestrel wrote: "Take decisive action to seize the objective — The Ashen Wake."
"Stand down, Mira. I'm done," the pilot says, and the voice has lost its patience. The Ashen Wake's engines gutter out. You close to point-blank and her guns stay dark. She hangs there, venting, with no heading left to run. Your hull is torn, but the fight is yours. The comm crackles again, and the pilot breathes once before speaking. "You'll want to hear who sent me."

Out past the Kobayashi IV's viewport, the dead hauler is a long way behind you now, and still it answers. A single pulse crawls across the scanner, then a second, small and steady: someone aboard the wreck is alive, and knocking on the hull from inside. The earlier silence was only the cargo bulkhead, which has been muffling them since the boarding. It is a poor hour for the news.

She is pulling a sealed ration tin back across the tabletop with two fingers, slowly, the way you retrieve a prize from something that might wake up. Last night's rumor was that the tin held peaches, and she has chosen to believe the rumor. Above the galley hatch hangs a small new apparition of condensation, a damp bloom spreading across the ceiling panel, exactly where she'd hoped there would be nothing at all. Mira has the Kobayashi IV's one working scanner turned toward the dead hauler's bearing, where a small steady knocking still crawls across the screen, and she is doing nothing about it. She is releasing the star-compass, in a sense: Ilse's brass compass sits open on the console, and she is gently easing its stiff little lid shut for the fifth time, as if closing it properly might count as a prayer. On the scanner's corner, behind the glass, a moth-sized insect has been caught between the screen and its cover, and it paces the narrow gap with great dignity, going nowhere at all. Mira taps the glass once, and it does not look up. Through the viewport the Cinder Wren hangs venting and dark, and its pilot has still not said who sent her.

You carry Ilse's brass star-compass, the one thing of hers you still have. It sits open on the console beside you now.

Tamsin Vey, the salvage broker with the ledger stall on the Hollow Spire docks, is the one you have a bond with; it stands at full strength. The story has not established any other dock trader as a friend.

You promised Tamsin Vey you would return to her stall on the Hollow Spire docks before the next tide of cargo. The story has not set that tide to any hour or day.
